sections.title: Not Following the Customs of the Gentiles
sections.html:
In many verses the Torah warned Israel not to follow the customs (ḥukot) of the gentiles, as it is stated (Vayikra 18:3): "You shall not copy the practices of the land of Egypt where you dwelt, nor shall you copy the practices of the land of Canaan to which I am bringing you, nor shall you follow their customs." It is likewise stated after the section on the forbidden sexual relations (Vayikra 20:22-24): "You shall keep all My statutes and all My laws and do them, so that the land to which I am bringing you to dwell in will not spew you out. You shall not follow the customs of the nation that I am driving out before you, for they did all these things and I loathed them. And I said to you: You shall possess their land, and I will give it to you to possess, a land flowing with milk and honey; I am the Lord your God, who has separated you from the peoples." It is likewise stated (Shemot 23:24): "You shall not bow down to their gods nor serve them, nor shall you act according to their practices…". And it is likewise stated (Devarim 12:30): "Beware lest you be ensnared to follow them after they have been destroyed before you, and lest you inquire about their gods, saying: How did these nations serve their gods? I too will do the same."

The meaning of the prohibition is that one should not try to imitate the gentiles in their customs in order to be like them, for example by dressing or cutting one's hair according to the garments and hairstyles that are distinctive to them, so that Israel will not be drawn after the culture and faith of the gentiles and abandon the mitzvot of the Torah. A 'ḥok' is a custom that has become so fixed that it has turned into a binding practice. In other words, beyond the prohibition against worshipping idols or honouring them, there is a prohibition against following the customs of the gentiles, that is, against resembling the gentiles by adopting customs that have become fixed in their culture.

Included in the prohibition is not to resemble the gentiles by performing acts based on superstitions. An example is cited in the Talmud (Shabbat 67b): there were gentiles who used to say to a raven when it called, "Scream!", and to a female raven, "Whistle, and turn your tail back to me for good." If they heard a rooster that called with the voice of a raven, or a hen that called with the voice of a rooster, they saw this as a bad sign and ordered that it be slaughtered. Likewise, one who drank a beverage would say, "I will drink and leave over, I will drink and leave over," as a charm so that drinking a little would benefit him like much. Similarly, people who raised chicks used to hurl eggs against a wall as a charm for the chicks' survival, and there were women who for this purpose danced before the chicks and counted seventy-one chicks. There were also customs of women connected to cooking food: when they prepared a dish of kutaḥ (a dip made with whey) they danced before the dish so that it would succeed; when they cooked lentils they silenced the people so that they would not spoil the cooking; when they cooked groats they shrieked so that they would cook well; and there were some who used to urinate before the dish so that it would succeed.

In the language of the Sages this prohibition is called 'the ways of the Emori' (Shabbat 67a-b), after the peoples of Canaan, who were also called by the general name 'Emorites'. Similarly, anyone who practises a gentile custom that has no logical explanation or proven benefit, so that it is reasonable to assume that it is based on idolatrous customs or on a superstitious belief that this custom will bring luck, transgresses the prohibition of "nor shall you follow their customs" and is liable to lashes.1

sections.title: The Parameters of the Prohibition
sections.html:
The prohibition is to learn from the gentiles customs that have no benefit, and whose entire reason for existing is that they are customs that became a statute of a foreign religion, or are done for the sake of licentiousness and arrogance (Maharik 88; BY and Rema YD 178:1).

Even with a gentile custom that is not connected to a foreign religion or to licentiousness, anyone who imitates it because he wishes to resemble the gentiles transgresses the prohibition (see the note).2

But if the gentiles' custom had a reason, it is permitted to do it, since one does not do it because it is a gentile custom but because of the logical benefit that may come from it. Therefore it was permitted to load stones onto trees that were shedding their fruit, because people held that by doing so the tree's strength would be weakened and it would have no surplus strength with which to shed its fruit. Likewise it is permitted to mark such trees with red paint, so that passers-by will see that they are sick and pray for them. Likewise it is permitted to do anything that people who practised medicine were accustomed to do for the sake of healing, even though these appear to be charm-like customs without reason, since in practice they are effective in the opinion of the healers (Shabbat 67a; below 29:1).

Similarly, the Sages permitted burning the personal articles of a king who died, even though the gentiles had this custom, because this custom has a reason – to express honour for the king who died, in that there is no other person worthy of using his articles (Avoda Zara 11a).

Similarly, the Rivash (158) permitted mourners to leave their homes and go to the cemetery every day, as was the custom of the Muslims, since this custom has a reason: it is done in honour of the deceased.

Likewise, the Maharik (88) permitted physicians to wear a special garment that the gentile physicians were particular to wear, so that patients would know that they were physicians and come to be treated by them for payment. Even though this was a gentile custom, and Jewish physicians in the past did not follow it, since the Jewish physicians wished to adopt it for the sake of their livelihood, there is no prohibition in this.3

sections.title: The Customs of the Gentiles in Hairstyles
sections.html:
It is forbidden to cut one's hair in a 'komi' style as idol worshippers used to do, who would shave the hair at the front of the head and grow it long at the back. Likewise it is forbidden to shave the hair around the head and leave the hair in the middle of the head. And anyone who cuts his hair in a manner distinctive to the gentiles transgresses the prohibition of "nor shall you follow their customs" and is liable to lashes (Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 11:1; SA YD 178:1). However, the Sages permitted a Jew who needed to be close to the government to have a 'komi' haircut and to dress like them, so that he could persuade them not to issue decrees against the Jews subject to them, for if he did not look like them they would despise him, and he would not succeed in acting on behalf of Israel (Bava Kamma 83a; SA YD 178:2).4

Some say that it is forbidden for men to grow long hair for the sake of adornment and pride, because this is an imitation of a gentile custom (Baḥ), for there were warriors in various countries who used to grow their hair long (Taz). And there were rabbis who warned young men against imitating other hairstyles that were widespread in the gentile society around them. On the other hand, there were those who defended those young men, holding that since they did not intend to imitate the gentiles but rather found it attractive, even though they learned it from the gentiles, there is no prohibition of 'the customs of the gentiles' in it. In addition, it is always a matter of a hairstyle that is not prevalent among all the gentiles in that place, and on the other hand there are also Jews who customarily wear it.

Several generations ago, many students of the Lithuanian yeshivot, and especially of the Slabodka school, were particular about their dignified appearance, so that it would look attractive even in the eyes of those who had left the Torah. To this end they wore a short modern suit in place of the long coat that had been customary until then, and they shaved their beards and grew a forelock above their foreheads and combed it according to the accepted fashion. When the Slabodka yeshiva moved to the Land of Israel (5684, 1924), there were members of the Old Yishuv who came out forcefully against them, claiming that they were influenced by modernity and were transgressing the Torah prohibition of following 'the customs of the gentiles'. But many held that there is no prohibition in this, because it is not a distinctly gentile custom that expresses religious or national affiliation, but rather this was how respectable young men conducted themselves at that time. Moreover, the heads of the yeshivot of the Slabodka school held that this dress had an advantage, for in a generation in which many young people were abandoning the way of the Torah and despising yeshiva students, it was fitting that yeshiva students should appear attractive and respectable in the eyes of all people.

In practice, any hairstyle that is also accepted among Jews and is not considered a distinctly gentile hairstyle involves no prohibition. When there is a distinctly gentile hairstyle, Jews who imitate it in order to resemble the gentiles transgress the prohibition of "nor shall you follow their customs". But if many Jews transgressed and adopted this hairstyle, since it has become prevalent among Jews too, it is no longer defined as a distinctly gentile custom, and the prohibition no longer applies to it.

As a rule, even when there is no outright prohibition of 'the customs of the gentiles', it is proper for a person not to imitate people who do not observe Torah and mitzvot, because the dress and hairstyle characteristic of those who observe Torah and mitzvot help him to walk in his path and to avoid foreign influences and passing fashions. In addition, there is Kiddush Hashem in a Jew declaring by his appearance that he is loyal to the Jewish people and its heritage.5

sections.title: The Customs of the Gentiles in Clothing
sections.html:
Included in the prohibition of "nor shall you follow their customs" is not to dress according to the custom distinctive to gentiles, and the prophet warned (Tzefanya 1:8) that those who do so will be punished, as it is stated: "And I will punish the officials and the king's sons, and all who wear foreign garments." The Sages said that Israel was redeemed from Egypt in the merit of not changing their dress (Pesikta Zutarta, Ki Tavo 46a). The Sages likewise expounded (in the Sifrei) on the verse (Devarim 12:30): "Beware lest you be ensnared to follow them after they have been destroyed before you, and lest you inquire about their gods…": "That you should not say: Since they go out in avtiga, I too will go out in avtiga; since they go out in purple, I too will go out in purple; since they go out in tulsin, I too will go out in tulsin" (Rambam, Sefer Ha-mitzvot, negative commandment 30).

We do not know what the garments mentioned by the Sages looked like, but it is agreed in halakha that it is forbidden to wear two kinds of gentile garments: the first, garments that gentiles customarily wear as part of their religious traditions, such as garments distinctive to the clergy of the various religions, as well as garments that members of religions customarily wear on their festivals, such as garments in special colours at Christmas or green garments on St Patrick's Day. The second kind is garments that gentiles customarily wear for the sake of licentiousness and arrogance, such as red purple garments in days gone by (Sifrei Devei Rav; Maharik; Rema YD 178:1).

But there is no prohibition for Jews to wear garments that the gentiles wore first, when the aim is not imitation but comfort or beauty. Therefore it is permitted for Jews to wear fashionable clothing, since they do so for the sake of beauty. However, in places where the Jews set themselves apart from the dress of the gentiles, one who changes the dress of the Jews in order to resemble the gentiles transgresses a Torah prohibition (Ḥokhmat Adam 89:1). But if they did not decide to set themselves apart from a particular garment, it involves no prohibition. For example, it is permitted for university students to wear a special gown at a graduation ceremony.

Even when Jews initially decided to set themselves apart from the gentiles regarding a certain garment, if Jews began to wear it, although the first ones transgressed the prohibition, once this garment has become prevalent among Jews there is no longer a prohibition in it (Beit Shlomo YD 197).

Inspired by the prohibition of 'the customs of the gentiles', many rabbis and educators warn their students not to imitate various gentile customs even though they do not fall within the bounds of the Torah prohibition, such as excessive devotion to sports teams and wearing their items of clothing, each community according to its circumstances.6

sections.title: Kippa
sections.html:
Some say that where Jews live among gentiles, a man who goes without a kippa transgresses the prohibition of "nor shall you follow their customs" (Mahari Bruna 34). On the other hand, according to many, those who go without a kippa do not transgress the prohibition of 'the customs of the gentiles', because the gentiles go without a head covering for reasons of comfort alone. Therefore going without a kippa is not a 'ḥok' of theirs.

However, all agree that it is right to be very particular about wearing a kippa, for wearing it strengthens religious identification and arouses the fear of Heaven, and there is also Kiddush Hashem in this, for one who wears a kippa thereby declares that it is an honour for him to be regarded as a faithful Jew.7

sections.title: Gentile Names
sections.html:
Some say that it is forbidden by Torah law to call children by gentile names that are not found among Jews, and likewise one whose parents gave him two names, one gentile and one Jewish, is forbidden to use the gentile name. For the Torah forbade resembling gentiles even in their dress and customs, and all the more so one should not resemble them in their names. We likewise learned from the words of the Sages (Bamidbar Rabba 13:20) that Israel was redeemed from Egypt in the merit of the fact "that they did not change their names, and did not change their language, and that they fenced themselves off from sexual immorality." But according to most poskim, although it is not proper to call a Jew by a distinctly gentile name, this does not involve an outright prohibition of 'the customs of the gentiles', since it is not done for the sake of a foreign religion or for the sake of licentiousness and arrogance (above, section 2). Therefore there is also no obligation for one who has two names, Jewish and gentile, to make sure that he is called specifically by the Jewish name.

All this is when the name is a distinctly gentile one that is not found among Jews, but if the gentile name has already taken root among Jews, according to all opinions there is no objection to using it. Indeed, we find that in all the exiles Jews were called by gentile names, among them rabbis and rabbis' wives, such as Rabbi Alexandri (Berakhot 17a), Rabbi Maimon the father of the Rambam, and Rabbi Vidal the author of the Maggid Mishneh. Likewise in Yiddish: Fishel, Ber, Gitel, Golda. And likewise in Sefarad: Fortuna. And although ideally it would have been proper for Jews to be called by names rooted in the Hebrew language, and in the opinion of many, the first ones who began calling their children by the gentile name did not act properly, once the name has taken root in Israel there is no objection to calling children by this name.8

sections.title: The Organ and Changing Customs in the Synagogue
sections.html:
On Sukkot of the year 5579 (1818), a 'Temple' was established in Hamburg, Germany, which later proved to have been the first Reform synagogue. At that time many German Jews, especially the young, were no longer careful about observing Shabbat and kashrut. The founders of the 'Temple' decided to adapt the prayers to the spirit of the young people of the modern generation, who had integrated into German society and did not understand Hebrew. To this end they shortened the prayers, removed passages relating to the sacrificial service, translated many passages into German, shortened the reading of the weekly Torah portion to a third, with the intention of completing the Torah in three years, and abolished the reading of the haftara. They also decided to accompany the prayers with organ playing by a gentile on Shabbat. They claimed that all the changes of custom they made were within the framework of halakha. But the dayanim of the city, and with them great rabbis from all over Central Europe, such as Rabbi Akiva Eiger and Rabbi Moshe Sofer, came out sharply against them, both because they were transgressing halakha and because of the grave concern that these changes would be the beginning of a disastrous process. About twenty-five years later, in 5604 (1844), the Reform movement took shape, which no longer purported to act within the framework of halakha but claimed that the mitzvot of the Torah that did not suit the spirit of enlightened German culture should be abolished. In those years in Germany, at least nine out of ten young people did not continue in the way of Yisrael Saba (the ancestral tradition of Israel), and most German Jews identified with the Reform movement (Masoret Ha-giyur p. 336).

As stated, in the first stage the dispute was whether the changes that the innovators introduced in the 'Hamburg Temple' were within the framework of halakha. In the following generations the dispute gradually spread to synagogues in other countries whose worshippers had been influenced by the Reformers but still wished to remain within the framework of halakha. The two stormy disputes were over bringing an organ into the synagogue and moving the bima to the front of the synagogue. Since one of the central arguments against these changes was that they involve the prohibition of 'the customs of the gentiles', we will mention them here briefly.

The organ is a musical instrument with a rich and moving sound, which Christians play in churches, and the Jewish innovators decided to accompany the prayers with it. In support of their initiative they cited the custom of the worshippers of a certain synagogue in Prague, who even before the dispute broke out used to accompany Kabbalat Shabbat with music. In addition, there was testimony about other synagogues in Italy and Frankfurt that did the same. They argued that although this custom was learned from the Christians, there is no prohibition of 'the customs of the gentiles' in it, since it is done in order to enrich the prayers and not in order to resemble them. In addition, the organ is not specific to Christian prayer and is used for other things as well. And since the aim is to enrich the prayers and to draw the young generation closer to prayer in the synagogue, there is a mitzva in it, and consequently it is permitted to ask a gentile to play on Shabbat, since this is a prohibition of 'shevut de-shevut' (a rabbinic prohibition upon a rabbinic prohibition), which is permitted for the sake of a mitzva.

But the vast majority of rabbis opposed very forcefully bringing an organ into the synagogue. Some held that it is forbidden by Torah law because of 'the customs of the gentiles', and some did not claim this, but held that from an educational standpoint it is forbidden to be drawn after the customs of the gentiles. In addition, since there is no mitzva in it, it is forbidden to ask a gentile to play on Shabbat. They further added that since the day the Temple was destroyed, where the Levites played music, it is not proper to create a substitute for their music in synagogues.

Meanwhile, a question arose for rabbis whose communities demanded that they bring an organ into the synagogue, and if they did not comply, Reform rabbis would be appointed in their place. In practice, in places where there was concern about the influence of the Reformers, most rabbis instructed the rabbis of those communities to resign and not to agree to bringing in an organ (Rav Hildesheimer; Melamed Le-ho'il 1:16). However, Rav Mordechai Horowitz wrote that since if he resigned a rabbi would come who would permit far worse things, "I cannot take upon myself and upon my neck the responsibility for all the mishaps that will result from this, Heaven forbid" (Mateh Levi OḤ 6). In Algeria, Rav David Ashkenazi did not abolish the custom, practised even before his time, of playing the organ in the great synagogue of Oran, and he wrote that it is better to fight over more important matters such as sheḥita and gittin (bills of divorce).9

sections.title: Changing the Location of the Bima in the Synagogue
sections.html:
The custom of Israel is to place the bima on which the Torah is read in the centre of the synagogue, so that everyone can hear the ḥazan well (Rambam, Hilkhot Tefila 11:2-4). However, Rabbi Yosef Karo wrote (Kesef Mishneh there) that this is not obligatory, and when there is a need, it may be placed at the side, and "everything depends on the place and the time."

The Reformers used to place the bima at the front of the synagogue, similar to churches, in which all the ceremonies take place at the front of the church. Many rabbis came out against changing the location of the bima, and wrote that even Rabbi Yosef Karo permitted changing the location of the bima only in a new synagogue, but where the bima had already been fixed in the past in the centre of the synagogue, the bima has acquired its place and it is forbidden to move it (Ḥatam Sofer OḤ 28; Imrei Esh OḤ 7). Later, people became more careful to keep away from the customs of the Reformers and feared that any change might undermine the foundations of religion, and even in a new synagogue, and even when there was a constraint, they did not agree to fixing the bima at the front of the synagogue (Meḥolat Ha-maḥanayim OḤ 5; Meshiv Davar OḤ 15). And there is one who explained that whenever there is space between the bima and the Holy Ark, such that one can circle the bima with the four species, there is no prohibition (Igrot Moshe OḤ 2:41).

Some ruled that it is preferable to pray alone than in a synagogue where the bima was moved forward (Maharam Schick OḤ 71; Yaskil Avdi part 7, OḤ 9). But according to many, one should not forbid praying in the synagogue because of this (Seridei Esh part 1, OḤ 15; Igrot Moshe OḤ 2:42). Moreover, in Muslim lands, where the Reformers had no influence, people were not particular about this matter, and when there was a need they placed the bima at the front of the synagogue (Yabi'a Omer part 8, OḤ 17). In practice, nowadays, when all the communities of Israel are intermingled, in case of need, such as in small synagogues, one may place the bima at the front of the synagogue, because by doing so one does not appear to be imitating the gentiles.

sections.title: Changes in Wedding Customs
sections.html:
Another change that the Reformers introduced was holding wedding ceremonies (ḥuppot) in the synagogue, like the Christians who held weddings in churches. Indeed, in the days of the Rishonim there were also Jews who used to hold ḥuppot in the synagogue (see Rema YD 391:3), but since over the years this custom ceased, and it appeared that the Reformers had introduced it in imitation of the Christian custom, the rabbis of Hungary rose up against it and forbade holding ḥuppot in the synagogue because of the prohibition of 'the customs of the gentiles' (Ktav Sofer EH 47; Maharam Schick EH 87; Meḥolat Ha-maḥanayim 4). And some forbade it because of the affront to the honour of the synagogue, which is designated for prayer and Torah alone (Imrei Esh OḤ 9). In consequence, other rabbis outside Hungary tended to forbid holding ḥuppot in the synagogue. However, in many communities in Muslim lands it was customary to hold ḥuppot in the synagogue.

In practice, when there is no intention to imitate the gentiles, it is permitted to hold a ḥuppa in the synagogue, on condition that the honour of the synagogue and the customs of modesty are preserved (Ta'alumot Lev part 3, 57; Igrot Moshe EH 1:93; Yabi'a Omer part 3, EH 10).

Later, following the rise of the feminist movement, the Reformers began to institute that at the ḥuppa the bride too would put a ring on the groom. But Rav Feinstein wrote that this involves a prohibition of 'the customs of the gentiles', for this is the Christian custom. In addition, people may mistakenly think that the kiddushin (betrothal) is effected by this (Igrot Moshe EH 3:18). On the other hand, some hold that this does not involve a prohibition of 'the customs of the gentiles', since it is not done in order to imitate the gentiles but to express the bride's partnership in the wedding. And although there is no prohibition of 'the customs of the gentiles' in it, it is right not to change the custom, and if the bride wishes to give the groom a ring, she should give it to him after the ḥuppa (the Rebbe Rayatz, Igrot Kodesh 8, 2284; Dibrot Eliyahu 12:158). It is worth noting that many God-fearing men customarily wear a wedding ring from the time of their marriage, in order to express that they are married and thereby to preserve their modesty.

sections.title: Changes in Funeral Customs
sections.html:
Another dispute arose regarding the funeral procession. The accepted custom was to place the deceased on a bier (stretcher) and to carry the bier by hand to the cemetery, and there were those who changed this and placed the bier on a black carriage, as was the custom of the gentiles. Many wrote that since the cities had grown and consequently the way to the cemetery had become longer, there is a reason for changing the custom, and therefore it involves no prohibition (Ktav Sofer YD 175). But there was one who forbade changing the custom and conveying the deceased in a carriage because of 'the customs of the gentiles' (Tuv Ta'am Va-da'at, Telita'ah 2:235). And there was one who forbade it when the carriage is black, like that of the gentiles (Beit She'arim YD 427).

Another dispute arose over planting trees and flowers around the grave. Some rabbis ruled that it is forbidden because of 'the customs of the gentiles' (Rav Hildesheimer; Har Tzvi YD 279). And some rabbis forbade it because it changes the custom (Melamed Le-ho'il 2:109; Beit She'arim YD 428).

Likewise, some forbade placing wreaths of flowers on the bier of the deceased or on the grave (Yaskil Avdi 4, YD 25). And some hold that there is no prohibition in this, since it is done in honour of the deceased and not in order to imitate the gentiles (Aseh Lekha Rav 1:44, and Responsa Mayim Ḥayim 3:27). And some agreed that there is no prohibition in it, but wrote that it is preferable not to change the custom and imitate the gentiles (Yabi'a Omer part 3, YD 24). Rav Goren did not protest against the military practice of laying wreaths, since this is done in all the armies of the world as a mark of honour and not as religious imitation; however, outside the framework of the army he wrote that it is not proper to lay wreaths (Terumat Ha-goren 84).10
